name: fast.cu (H100 BF16 matmul and sum-reduction kernels)
baseline: cuBLAS (cublasGemmEx, BF16 inputs, FP32 compute, CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT) for matmul; CUB for sum reduction
workload: Square bf16 matrix multiplication with fp32 accumulation at N=4096 and N=8192, plus a sum over 2^30 elements, all on an H100.
claimed_speedup: Matmul N=4096: 763 TFLOPs vs cuBLAS 716 TFLOPs (about 1.07x, derived from page data); N=8192: 808 vs 795 TFLOPs (about 1.02x, derived from page data). Sum of 2^30 elements: 3240.11 GB/s vs CUB 3193 GB/s (about 1.01x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -w --use_fast_math --expt-relaxed-constexpr --expt-extended-lambda -gencode arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a, linked with -lcublas -lcuda (from the repo Makefile); CUDA toolkit version not stated
hardware: NVIDIA H100 (SXM or PCIe variant, clocks and host CPU not stated)
tradeoffs: Hopper-only (sm_90a); BF16 square matrices with FP32 accumulation; orchestration in h100/matmul.cu with example kernels in h100/matmul/, tuned for specific sizes rather than a general GEMM API. The repo also carries GB300 NVFP4 GEMM kernels that need CUDA 13.1 and a GB300/B300.
caveats: Margins over cuBLAS are small (about 7% at N=4096, about 2% at N=8192) and only two sizes are reported. README does not state CUDA version, H100 variant, clocks or CPU, so the tier A rests on public harness (h100/matmul.cu checks correctness against cublasGemmEx and prints TFLOPS) plus Makefile flags; a verifier may want to downgrade. The worklog blog post (cudaforfun.substack.com, 'Outperforming cuBLAS on H100') could not be opened (egress blocked); its numbers were read from the README and a search snippet.
found_via: WebSearch 'outperforming cuBLAS on H100 worklog matmul kernel from scratch' (Substack worklog 'Outperforming cuBLAS on H100: a Worklog' and the author's X post), then opened the repo and README

name: FastGEMV (fp16/int8/int4 GEMV CUDA kernels)
baseline: PyTorch fp16 matrix-vector product (torch.matmul on a size x size fp16 matrix and size x 1 vector, baseline.py, kernel time via Nsight Systems)
workload: GEMV of an n x n fp16 matrix with an n x 1 fp16 vector for n=512..16384, plus int8 and int4 quantized-matrix variants that PyTorch cannot run directly; kernel runtime and estimated memory bandwidth.
claimed_speedup: README: max 2.7x speedup vs PyTorch on P100 and 1.4x on 3090 Ti. method_and_result.md, P100 fp16: 1.441x (n=512), 1.627x (1024), 1.551x (2048), 1.599x (4096), 2.695x (8192), 1.781x (16384); estimated bandwidth 602.0 GB/s vs PyTorch 320.8 GB/s at n=16384 (peak 732 GB/s). RTX 3090 fp16 kernel: 4372.4 ns vs PyTorch 6106.2 ns at n=1024 (about 1.40x, derived from page data); 609235 ns vs 691660.6 ns at n=16384 (about 1.14x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 -m64 -std=c++17 with -gencode sm_60/sm_70/sm_75/sm_86 (Makefile); README requirements list CUDA 11.7 and Nsight Systems 2023.1.2; PyTorch version not stated
hardware: NVIDIA P100 and RTX 3090 (README says 3090 Ti, results doc says 3090); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Square power-of-two sizes only (512..16384); per-tensor scale and zero point for int8/int4; blockDim must be tuned per size and GPU; no batching; tested on Pascal and Ampere only.
caveats: Benchmarks date from May-June 2023 against the PyTorch and cuBLAS of that time; modern PyTorch on Ada/Hopper may have closed the gap. The 2.7x peak is a single size (n=8192) on a P100; on the 3090 the gain is 1.1-1.4x. The int8/int4 columns compare against fp16 PyTorch and move far fewer bytes, so they are not like-for-like. README names a 3090 Ti while the results document says 3090. Timings are Nsight Systems kernel sums, not end-to-end wall clock. Host CPU not stated. Tier A is a judgment call: harness and flags are public, but PyTorch version and CPU are missing.
found_via: github.com/topics/cuda-kernels?l=cuda listing (description 'at most 2.7x speedup compared to pytorch baseline'), then opened repo, README, Makefile, baseline.py and method_and_result.md

name: bare-metal (hand-optimized SASS/CUDA ML kernels for RTX 3070 Ti Laptop)
baseline: cuBLAS (local reference harness; cuDNN and cuSPARSELt rows also measured and lost)
workload: FP16 tensor-core HGEMM (16-warp kernel) on square 2048^3 and 4096^3 problems, against cuBLAS measured on the same RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU under a no-throttle fair-run policy (median of 11 runs after 5 warmups).
claimed_speedup: HGEMM 16-warp 2048^3: 31,875 GFLOPS vs cuBLAS 28,631 GFLOPS (111.3%); 4096^3: 31,765 vs 29,708 GFLOPS (106.9%). The same table shows the project losing elsewhere: dense INT8 GEMM 68.7% of cuBLAS, sparse INT8 25.4% and 18.2% of cuSPARSELt, conv2d implicit GEMM 42.3% of cuDNN.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -arch=sm_86 -O2 (kernels via --cubin, bench harnesses use the CUDA Driver API; reference benches add -std=c++17 and link cublas, cublasLt, cudnn, cusparseLt); CUDA 13.2 (nvcc V13.2.78) per AGENTS.md
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU (GA104, sm_86) under a 150 W VBIOS cap; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: sm_86 (Ampere GA104) only; kernels are compiled to cubin and some are hand-edited at SASS level through the project's R package cuasmR, so they are not portable C++ source; reproduction needs CUDA, Nsight and R (make reproduce).
caveats: Only the two square HGEMM rows beat cuBLAS; every other row in the same table loses. Single laptop GPU with a power cap; README says several results are n=1 and that the repo disputes one of its own numbers with an open issue and footnote (29 open issues). Reference numbers recorded 2026-05-18. cuBLAS heuristics on this laptop part may be suboptimal, so the margin may not transfer to desktop GPUs. Tier A rests on the public reproducible harness (make reproduce, data/reference_baselines.json) plus stated flags and CUDA version; host CPU not stated. Flash Attention rows have no cuDNN reference locally ('not measured locally').
found_via: github.com/topics/flash-attention?l=cuda and github.com/topics/gemm?l=cuda listings ('hand-tuned NVIDIA SASS kernels ... no cuBLAS / cuDNN / PyTorch'), then opened README, docs/comparison_to_sota.md, AGENTS.md, Makefile and data/reference_baselines.json

name: Mini-Attention (FlashAttention-2 from scratch in CUDA C++ for SM120)
baseline: cuDNN fused attention via PyTorch SDPA (SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION)
workload: FP16 attention forward on an RTX 5090 (SM120) for sequence lengths N=512..8192; the README's NCU section uses B=2, H=8, N=1024, D=128 but the latency table's shape is not stated.
claimed_speedup: K7 vs cuDNN latency: N=512 0.185 ms vs 0.247 ms (133.2% of cuDNN throughput); N=1024 0.658 vs 0.739 ms (112.2%); N=2048 2.588 vs 2.515 ms (97.2%); N=4096 5.201 vs 4.945 ms (95.1%); N=8192 10.310 vs 9.904 ms (96.1%). README headline: 'K7 beats cuDNN by 12-35% at N<=1024; reaches 97-100% of cuDNN at N>=2048'.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5090 (SM120 Blackwell, 419 TFLOPS FP16 peak, 1792 GB/s); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: FP16 forward only, head dim 128 kernels, consumer Blackwell (SM120) and SM86 ports; hand-tuned PTX (mma.sync, ldmatrix, cp.async) in CUDA C++; benchmarks driven from Python and PyTorch; SM100/B200 kernel is work in progress.
caveats: Wins only at short sequences (N<=1024) and is 3-5% slower than cuDNN from N=2048 up. README tables disagree: the first table gives K7/cuDNN 133.2% and 112.2% at N=512 and 1024, the progression table gives 134.7% and 114.4%. Batch, heads and head dim of the latency table, compiler flags and CUDA version are not stated. cuDNN is called through PyTorch SDPA, so dispatch overhead may inflate the relative win at the smallest shapes. No license file in the repo root, so code must not be copied. First-party numbers, 1 star, about 9 days of commit history.
found_via: WebSearch 'attention kernel written from scratch CUDA C++ beats cuDNN flash attention benchmark blog'

name: Flash Attention PTX/CUDA (hand-written PTX prefill attention for RTX 5080)
baseline: FlashAttention-2 as bundled in vLLM 0.23.0 (vllm.vllm_flash_attn.flash_attn_varlen_func, FA2 path)
workload: Causal fp16 attention prefill over 34 shapes (B=1..8, H=12 or 32, S=512..8192, D=64 or 128) on an RTX 5080, same-process interleaved timing with shared random inputs; plus end-to-end Qwen2.5-1.5B decode and prefill against vLLM.
claimed_speedup: Beats or matches vLLM FA2 at 23 of 34 shapes. Latency-based gains: D=64 H=12 B=1 +18.5% (S=512), +31.9% (S=1024), +8.9% (S=2048); D=128 H=12 B=1 +16.6% (S=512), +12.6% (S=1024). Losses up to -4.8% (B=8 S=4096 D=64) and -4.5% (B=8 S=8192 D=128). Peak about 202 TFLOPS vs vLLM about 212. End-to-end Qwen2.5-1.5B decode B=1: 4.70 ms/token vs vLLM 5.12 ms/token; B=8: 5.28 vs 5.43 ms/step.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build, CUDA Toolkit 12.0+ (tested with 13.1), C++17, sm_120; full nvcc flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5080 (84 SMs, sm_120, 234.8 TFLOPS FP16 theoretical), Windows/WSL2 for the vLLM comparison; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Consumer Blackwell (sm_120) only; mma.sync-based, no WGMMA/TMA; forward/prefill kernels with paged-KV decode glue; PyTorch bindings (fa_ptx) and a C++ API; the default branch shown on GitHub is dev/FlashAtt.
caveats: Loses at the largest batch x context shapes (-2 to -5%) and wins mainly at B=1 and short or mid context. The same-process vLLM harness (fa_sweep2.py) lives in the author's WSL environment and is not in the repo, so the comparison is not reproducible from the repo alone (hence tier C); in-repo benchmark is src/bench.cu. Baseline is FlashAttention-2 because FA3 does not run on sm_120; no cuDNN comparison. Single GPU, first-party, history of about one week.
found_via: WebSearch 'attention kernel written from scratch CUDA C++ beats cuDNN flash attention benchmark blog' (surfaced the repo), then opened README and docs/vllm-comparison.md

name: llm.c (GPT-2/GPT-3 training in C/CUDA)
workload: GPT-2 pretraining step throughput of the mainline train_gpt2.cu against a PyTorch implementation; model size, batch, GPU and PyTorch version are not stated in the README.
claimed_speedup: 'Currently, llm.c is a bit faster than PyTorch Nightly (by about 7%).'
tradeoffs: GPT-2/GPT-3 family only; hand-written forward and backward passes (no general autodiff); the README says mainline uses cuBLAS for matmuls and keeps the root code simple, with experimental faster kernels in dev/cuda; a reference CPU fp32 version is in train_gpt2.c.
caveats: Single-sentence first-party claim with no GPU model, CUDA version, flags, batch size or raw numbers on the page; the PyTorch nightly of that time is not identified and the gap may have changed since the repo went quiet in May 2025. The win comes from fused custom kernels and absence of framework overhead while matmuls still go through cuBLAS.
found_via: Direct check of well-known 'faster than PyTorch' projects while searching 'fast ML kernel engineering blog beating cuDNN oneDNN'; opened repo page and README

name: XNNPACK (vs TensorFlow Lite built-in CPU kernels)
workload: TensorFlow Lite model inference on mobile and x86 CPUs with the XNNPACK delegate enabled compared with TFLite's default kernels.
claimed_speedup: Per TensorFlow Blog 'Accelerating TensorFlow Lite with XNNPACK Integration' as seen in a WebSearch snippet only: on average 2.3X faster floating-point inference; on x86 about 5X faster on average, with low-end and older processors over 20X.
compiler_and_flags: Repo README benchmarks used end2end_bench --benchmark_min_time=5 on an Android/ARM64 build with Android NDK r21 (bazel build -c opt --config android_arm64); flags of the blog comparison not seen
hardware: Repo README table: Pixel, Pixel 2, Pixel 3a phones and Raspberry Pi 2/3/4 boards (absolute MobileNet times only); blog hardware not seen
stars_or_usage: 2.5k stars; backend of TensorFlow Lite, PyTorch Mobile, ONNX Runtime and MediaPipe
tradeoffs: Operator library (not a standalone runtime) with NHWC layout and 40+ operators, meant to be embedded by frameworks; ARM64, ARMv7, x86/x86-64, WebAssembly, RISC-V and Hexagon targets.
caveats: XNNPACK is itself one of the baselines named for this category; it is listed here only for its claim over TFLite's own kernels. The blog post (blog.tensorflow.org, 2020-07) and its sequel on quantized inference could not be opened (egress blocked), so the speedup figures are snippet only and the repo README carries absolute MobileNet latencies without a comparison column. Numbers are from 2020 against TFLite of that era.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ tensor contraction OR convolution library outperforms Eigen Tensor OR XNNPACK OR oneDNN benchmark blog post' (TensorFlow Blog result), then opened the repo page, commits page, README and LICENSE

name: Kaoken (baked-weight C code generation for CPU transformer inference)
baseline: PyTorch CPU layers (transformers GPT-2 building blocks)
workload: Per-layer CPU timings of GPT-2 blocks at batch 1 (LayerNorm [1,768], GELU [1,768], Linear [768,50257], Attention [1,768]), average of five runs, no GPU.
claimed_speedup: PyTorch vs Kaoken in ms: LayerNorm 0.052 vs 0.0052; GELU 0.174 vs 0.084; Linear 22.4 vs 2.378; Attention 14.484 vs 9.386 (about 10x, 2.1x, 9.4x and 1.5x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Weights are baked into generated source and matmuls are unrolled into straight-line code, so each model needs its own generated, very large C file; only GPT-2 layers implemented; CPU only; Python tooling required to generate.
caveats: CPU model, compiler and flags, thread counts and PyTorch version are not stated; per-layer microbenchmarks at batch 1 rather than end-to-end inference, where PyTorch per-op overhead dominates LayerNorm and GELU; README headline still says 'by X%' (placeholder); about one month of commit history; first-party.
found_via: WebSearch 'Kaoken handcrafted layer implementations CPU inference faster than PyTorch github' following a Show HN result ('Show HN: Speed up model inference on CPU with hand crafted layer implementations')

name: CodeJeNN (Keras-to-C++ inference header generator)
baseline: Keras eager-mode inference (TensorFlow backend for the MLP case, PyTorch backend for the CNN case)
workload: Single-thread, single-core inference of a small MLP and CNN, 10,000 loops each on fresh random samples, generated C++ vs Keras eager (and Keras JIT mode).
claimed_speedup: From a WebSearch summary of the arXiv paper 2607.02746 (paper not opened, snippet only): roughly 25x faster than Keras with the TensorFlow backend and nearly 38x with the PyTorch backend; about 2.5x and 9x faster than the JIT-enabled TensorFlow and PyTorch versions. The repo itself holds no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: GCC from Homebrew (not Apple clang) in a conda environment with llvm-openmp; optimization flags not stated
hardware: MacBook with M1 Pro chip, single thread on one core
tradeoffs: Emits a standalone C++ header with inlined static weights and no Lapack or Eigen dependency; large models can become memory-bandwidth bound because of big static arrays (noted in the repo); input must be a Keras HDF5 model with supported layers only.
caveats: Speedup figures were not read on an opened page (arXiv blocked), so they are snippet-level and the two summaries seen were not identical in detail; the repo's speed test (tutorials/06_speed_test, run.sh) reproduces the setup but publishes no numbers. License is the NRL Open License (use and modify allowed, redistribution only under that agreement, grant-back of modifications to the US Government), which is not an OSI license, so treated as reference. Single commit in history. Baseline is Keras eager mode, which is slow for tiny models, so the comparison favors generated code.
found_via: WebSearch 'Show HN faster than PyTorch kernels written from scratch C++ CUDA OR CPU inference engine benchmark' restricted to news.ycombinator.com (surfaced the arXiv paper title), then WebSearch 'CodeJeNN github C++ neural network generator ...'

name: Chipmunk (column-sparse attention and MLP kernels for diffusion transformers)
baseline: FlashAttention-3 (attention layer) and cuBLAS / torch.compile'd nn.Sequential (MLP layer); torch.compile'd reference repos for end-to-end
workload: Dynamic column-sparse attention and MLP layers inside HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1, FLUX.1-dev and Mochi diffusion-transformer inference on H100 GPUs; layer-level and end-to-end video/image generation latency.
claimed_speedup: 'Column Sparse Attention layer is ~9.3x faster than FlashAttention3 baseline; Column Sparse MLP layer is ~2.5x faster than cuBLAS baseline.' End-to-end: HunyuanVideo 720x1280x129 Chipmunk alone 1030 s -> 477 s (2.16x); Chipmunk + step caching 277 s on 1xH100 (3.72x) and 412 s on 8xH100 (2.50x); Wan2.1 up to 2.67x; FLUX.1-dev about 1.6x.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit >= 12.4 (12.8 recommended), conda cuda 12.8.0, torch.compile for baselines; nvcc flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA H100 (1x and 8x), Hopper required for the CUDA kernels; Ampere supported via Triton ports; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Approximate and training-free: it skips attention and MLP work by dynamic sparsity (column-sparse deltas against cached activations), so outputs differ from dense baselines (README reports VBench quality scores); Hopper-only CUDA kernels plus Triton ports; needs per-model integration; PyTorch-based.
caveats: Layer speedups compare a sparse method with dense baselines at undisclosed sparsity levels in the README; the microbenchmark scripts behind the 9.3x and 2.5x figures were not located, and the README's benchmark baselines are torch.compile'd reference repos. Workshop papers only (ES-FoMo at ICML 2025, YPS at MLSys 2025). Not a drop-in exact kernel replacement.
found_via: github.com/topics/cuda-kernels?l=cuda listing (description 'ColumnSparseGEMM 2.5x vs cuBLAS'), then opened repo, README and commits page

name: yalm (Yet Another Language Model, C++/CUDA LLM inference)
baseline: Hugging Face transformers (PyTorch) GPU inference; llama.cpp GPU also measured
workload: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 in FP16 with 4k context, decode tokens per second averaged over ~120-token and ~4800-token generations on an RTX 4090.
claimed_speedup: yalm 63.8 and 58.7 tok/s vs huggingface transformers 25.9 and 25.7 tok/s (about 2.5x and 2.3x, derived from page data). vs llama.cpp 61.0 and 58.8 tok/s: about +4.6% at ~120 tokens and a tie at ~4800 tokens (derived from page data). calm (66.0 and 65.7 tok/s) is faster than yalm.
tradeoffs: Educational, not for production per its README: single GPU, completions only (no chat interface), a few model families (Mistral-7B, Mixtral, Llama-3.2), requires converting safetensors weights to its own .yalm format.
caveats: Only the margin over Hugging Face transformers is large; against llama.cpp it is within 5% and the README shows another engine (calm) ahead. Versions and flags of transformers and llama.cpp and the compile flags of yalm are not stated; no LICENSE file appeared in the repo root listing, so the code is treated as reference. The author's blog post 'Fast LLM Inference From Scratch' (andrewkchan.dev) was not opened.
found_via: github.com/topics/inference-engine?l=c%2B%2B listing ('LLM inference in C++/CUDA, no libraries except for I/O'), then opened repo, README and commits page

name: XAD (Xcelerit ad-benchmarks suite results)
baseline: CppAD, Adept 2 and autodiff (C++ automatic differentiation libraries), plus finite differences
workload: Gradient (all sensitivities) time on four quant-finance kernels: Heston Monte Carlo (8 sensitivities), SABR calibration (15), XVA CVA (40) and LIBOR swaption (161), reverse mode, median of 10 iterations after warmup, 10K MC paths.
claimed_speedup: Gradient time, XAD tape vs CppAD / Adept / autodiff: Heston MC 40 ms vs 268 / 91 ms / did not finish; SABR 8.4 ms vs 32 / 19 / 38 ms; XVA CVA 2.6 s vs 8.0 / 7.1 s / did not finish; LIBOR swaption 1.00 s vs 4.57 / 1.15 s / did not finish. README: XAD tape is the fastest tape library on every benchmark (about 1.1x vs Adept on LIBOR up to 2.3x vs Adept on Heston); the commercial XAD-Codegen backend is 2x-5x faster than XAD tape (21 ms, 4.9 ms, 0.57 s, 0.31 s).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3, -O3 -mavx2 -mfma, identical flags across libraries (CMake Release)
tradeoffs: XAD is AGPL-3.0 (commercial licensing and enterprise support sold by Xcelerit); the fastest results use xad-codegen, which is commercially licensed and AVX2-only; tape-based adjoint mode with higher memory use than forward mode.
caveats: Evidence for the already-catalogued XAD, not a new project. The suite was written by the XAD vendor (Xcelerit, commits by auto-differentiation-dev) with only four finance workloads; the tier A rests on public code, compiler, flags and CPU being stated. autodiff did not finish three of four benchmarks. Last commit date shown for XAD itself; the ad-benchmarks repo has a single commit from 2026-04-12.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ reverse-mode automatic differentiation library blog benchmark faster than PyTorch Enzyme Stan CppAD' (surfaced reach2sayan/ad-benchmarks, a copy of the Xcelerit suite), then opened the canonical auto-differentiation/ad-benchmarks and XAD pages
